situation:
You are the licensing manager and the compliance manager at LOOPWORKS SOFTWARE COOPERATIVE, a consumer app developer owned and operated by the people who work there. LoopWorks built a personal-finance app that layers an environmental-impact score onto everyday purchases, and the score has become the feature outside clients most want to license. The general manager (judge) has asked the two of you to review one pending licensing decision and recommend how to proceed.

LoopWorks protects the scoring algorithm as a trade secret rather than a patent, since patenting would require publishing the method the co-op considers its real advantage. Two existing clients already use the score under limited, non-exclusive agreements: a regional grocery chain that prints it on shelf tags, and an overseas appliance manufacturer that cites it on packaging sold abroad. Both agreements promised each client priority partnership status once LoopWorks was ready to expand licensing, without defining what priority would mean in practice.

Both clients have now asked for exclusive rights, and the two requests cannot both be granted. The grocery chain wants the score kept off any competitor's shelves nationwide. The manufacturer wants exclusive rights abroad, where a foreign environmental-marketing regulator is reviewing whether the score's claims meet that country's administrative rules before it can be printed on any product sold there. Granting either client exclusivity would require breaking the priority promise made to the other.

The manufacturer relationship carries extra weight: LoopWorks spent a year and a substantial share of its member-approved budget adapting the algorithm's data exports to satisfy that country's import and disclosure rules, a cost the co-op justified against a forecast that overseas licensing revenue would grow steadily once the regulator cleared the score. That regulator's decision is still pending, and nothing in the forecast holds if the manufacturer walks away over an exclusivity dispute before the review concludes. The grocery chain's domestic business carries no comparable regulatory uncertainty.

LoopWorks has built its brand on member ownership and on customers trusting the score more than a competitor's, and the general manager (judge) worries that mishandling either client damages that trust with the consumers who see the score every day. The general manager (judge) wants you to recommend which client, if either, should receive exclusive rights, and how LoopWorks should manage its relationship with whichever client does not receive them.

The general manager (judge) will greet you and your partner at the start of the meeting and ask to hear your recommendation. The general manager (judge) will listen to your full presentation, then ask questions about the recommendation and about how LoopWorks should carry it out, and will thank you both once the presentation and the questions are finished.

judgeQuestions: If we grant one client exclusive rights, what should we do next to keep the relationship with the other client from breaking down?
